extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, employers, safety professionals, label preparers, and compliance officers
extracted.subtask_short: OSHA HCS labeling and SDS compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for updating labels, small-container labeling, safety data sheet (SDS) content and storage, and trade secret (CBI) disclosures under the OSHA Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional label-update accommodation for chemicals released for shipment (f)(11)
rubrics_metrics.description: For chemicals that have been released for shipment and are awaiting further distribution, the chemical manufacturer, importer, or distributor has the option not to relabel after learning significant new hazard information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the manufacturer/importer/distributor chooses this optional accommodation they must produce updated labels for each container and send those labels with the shipment for the downstream users. This accommodation is intended to avoid the burdens and hazards of relabeling containers in a narrow set of circumstances; manufacturers can opt instead to update the label at the point of shipment if concerned about liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility of originator to ensure updated labels accompany shipment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the responsibility of the originator to ensure updated labels accompany the shipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA clarifies that manufacturers, distributors and importers can always follow the requirements for updating labels as laid out in the first part of (f)(11). The provision is optional; originators concerned about liability may choose not to use the accommodation and instead relabel at shipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that updated labels be sent with the shipment (not separately)
rubrics_metrics.description: Updated labels must be sent together with every shipped container when using the optional accommodation; sending labels separately or relying on the SDS is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA rejected suggestions to allow labels to be sent electronically or in advance or to rely on SDSs, reasoning that allowing the label to be sent separately would fail to ensure downstream users have the updated label with each container. Because the provision is optional, manufacturers lacking mechanisms to provide labels with the shipment can instead relabel each container prior to shipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'released for shipment' and scope of the accommodation
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA is adding a definition of 'released for shipment' to clarify applicability of the accommodation in (f)(11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The accommodation applies to any container filled, sealed, and labeled by the manufacturer before the expiration of the six‑month deadline and applies to containers within an immediate outer package as long as the immediate outer package is already 'released for shipment'. Immediate containers still must be packaged for shipment to meet the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to include a 'release for shipment' date on the label
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA has decided not to adopt its proposed requirement to include the 'release for shipment' date on the label in this final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters conditioned support on eliminating or adjusting the correlating proposed requirement to add the date; OSHA declined to adopt such a date requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-container labeling accommodation eligibility (f)(12) — feasibility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The small container labeling provisions apply only where the chemical manufacturer, importer, or distributor can demonstrate that it is not feasible to use pull-out labels, fold-back labels, or tags containing the full label information required by paragraph (f)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA requires a showing of infeasibility (e.g., space considerations or extraordinary economic considerations). New paragraph (f)(12) would not require prior approval—only that the company must demonstrate that the full label was infeasible. OSHA maintains that wherever possible full label information should be on the immediate container.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum label elements for small containers ≤100 ml (f)(12)(ii)(A)-(E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Labels on small containers that are less than or equal to 100 milliliter (ml) capacity must include, at minimum: product identifier; pictogram(s); signal word; chemical manufacturer's name and phone number; and a statement that the full label information for the hazardous chemical is provided on the immediate outer package.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This accommodation mirrors examples in GHS Annex 7 and aligns with Health Canada's HPR small-capacity requirements. OSHA rejected removal of the U.S. phone number requirement because it provides workers immediate access to additional information if the SDS is not in the immediate vicinity. OSHA also does not require explicit SDS references on the small container label because space is at a premium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption for very small containers ≤3 ml (f)(12)(iii)
rubrics_metrics.description: No labels are required for small containers of 3 ml capacity or less where the chemical manufacturer, importer, or distributor can demonstrate that any label would interfere with the normal use of the container; however, if a container meets the conditions and no label is required, the container must bear, at minimum, the product identifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the product identifier could be etched on a 3 ml glass vial to ensure the identifier remains fixed to the vial. OSHA selected 3 ml as the cut-off for total exemption and declined requests to raise it to 5 ml.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate outer package label requirements for small containers (f)(12)(iv)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any small container covered by paragraph (f)(12)(ii) or (iii), the immediate outer package must include the full label information required by paragraph (f)(1) for each hazardous chemical in the immediate outer package, along with a statement that the small container(s) inside must be stored in the immediate outer package bearing the complete label when not in use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision also states that labels affixed to the immediate outer package must not be removed or defaced, as required by existing paragraph (f)(9). OSHA provides multiple flexibilities (pull-out labels, tags, etc.) and shows kit-labeling options in Annex 7 (example 10—scenario A and B). OSHA declined suggestions to shift relabeling responsibility to downstream users in mixed-kit scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with other jurisdictions is desirable but worker protection is primary
rubrics_metrics.description: While OSHA considered alignment with Canada's HPR and other jurisdictions, OSHA will not remove required information on the immediate outer package if that would reduce worker protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA chose the 100 ml cut-off partly to align with Canada's requirements. But OSHA declined suggestions to remove outer-package full label information solely for harmonization reasons when it would reduce protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: SDS language: SDS must be in English (g)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chemical manufacturer or importer shall ensure that the safety data sheet is in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a technical clarification intended to ensure consistency with paragraph (g)(1) which permits obtaining rather than preparing SDSs.

rubrics_metrics.name: SDS storage: allow SDSs to be stored to cover groups while preserving individual 16-section format (g)(10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (g)(10) revised to allow SDSs to be stored, rather than designed, in a way that covers groups of hazardous chemicals in a work area, while maintaining the standardized 16-section SDS format for each chemical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers can no longer 'design' SDSs that address groups of hazardous chemicals; they must maintain individual 16-section SDSs but may store them grouped by work area. OSHA will issue guidance and respond to inquiries. Electronic access is permitted provided it poses no barriers to immediate employee access and employers can immediately provide copies to medical personnel (consistent with (g)(8)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single SDS for similar complex mixtures allowed (g)(4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (g)(4) allows chemical importers, manufacturers and retailers to prepare a single SDS where complex mixtures have similar hazards and contents (i.e., the chemical ingredients are essentially the same, but the specific composition varies from mixture to mixture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a single SDS is used for similar mixtures or in cases of batch-to-batch variability, concentration ranges of ingredients may be used. If composition differences are small and hazards remain the same, ranges may be used; separate SDSs are required for blends containing distinct ingredients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secret (CBI) — allow withholding concentration ranges and require prescribed concentration ranges (i)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed to allow manufacturers, importers, and employers to withhold a chemical's concentration range as a trade secret and to require the use of prescriptive concentration ranges in lieu of the actual concentration or concentration range whenever the actual concentration or concentration range is claimed as a trade secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed prescribed ranges align with Canada's WHMIS. OSHA requested comments on whether these ranges provide sufficient information for downstream manufacturers and workers, and considered alternatives (more lenient or more restrictive combinations). Stakeholders expressed support and concerns regarding CBI protection, potential for ranges to cross hazard classification thresholds, and potential compliance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the narrowest applicable prescribed concentration range; combining consecutive ranges for 0.1–30% window (i)(1)(v)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed new paragraph (i)(1)(v) would require use of the narrowest applicable concentration range, but when the concentration to be withheld falls between 0.1 percent and 30 percent and does not fit entirely into one prescribed range, would permit use of a single range created by the combination of two applicable consecutive ranges instead—provided the combined range does not include any range entirely outside the actual concentration range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA sought comments on this approach and on two alternatives: allowing combinations among all ranges up to 100 percent (more lenient) or allowing combinations only for ranges up to 10 percent (more restrictive). Commenters raised issues about ranges being too narrow to protect CBI or overlapping/crossing hazard thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace 'physician and nurse' with 'Physician or other licensed health care professional (PLHCP)' (i)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed to replace the phrase 'physician and nurse' in paragraph (i) with the term 'Physician or other licensed health care professional (PLHCP)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA defines PLHCP as an individual whose legally permitted scope of practice (license, registration, or certification) allows the individual to independently provide or be delegated the responsibility to provide some or all of the health care services referenced in paragraph (i) of the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer requirement: SDS accessibility (g)(8) reiterated in context of (g)(10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must maintain copies of the required SDSs for each hazardous chemical and make sure they are readily accessible to employees when in their work areas; electronic access is permitted if it poses no barriers to immediate employee access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA's revision to (g)(10) does not change (g)(8). Employers providing SDSs electronically must ensure immediate employee access and ability to provide copies to medical personnel when needed.
